speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the course of our work as Members of Parliament, we would have come across households seeking help and assistance, as they juggle the many roles expected of a family: breadwinner, caregiver to elderly parents, and parents to young or teenage children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It gets harder when elderly parents lose mental capacity because of dementia or become bedridden because of illness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Double the challenge if they have children with disability or special needs to provide for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through various schemes and programmes, we want to better enable our families as they carry out their caregiving roles as the first line of care and protection for their vulnerable members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, one of the key priorities for the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and the Ministry of Health (MOH), both now and in the years ahead, is to enhance support for the elderly and people with disability and special needs, and to better enable their family members and loved ones to carry out their roles as caregivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: From time to time, we hear about sad cases where elderly persons or persons with disability or special needs are abused or neglected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, we have in place a network of community and social service agencies which support families through social intervention, such as counselling, case management and case monitoring.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not her real name; we will not use any real names in this Chamber on this topic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When neighbours spotted Mdm Chua wandering around the estate with bruises on her arms and around her left eye, they alerted the Family Service Centre (FSC).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The FSC found out that Mdm Chua’s daughter would beat her mother every time Mdm Chua soiled herself or left the stove on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When social workers contacted the daughter, she expressed remorse for using force against her mother.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We found out that the daughter’s anger stemmed from her frustration and stress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Not only was she coping badly with her mother’s failing health, she also needed to care for her own son who has special needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The daughter agreed to participate in counselling and assistance programmes to help her manage Mdm Chua’s failing mental and physical health.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To provide the daughter with caregiver respite, the FSC also persuaded another of Mdm Chua’s daughters to step in to care for Mdm Chua on weekdays.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assistance was also given to help her care for her son, who had special needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since our involvement, there have not been further incidents of violence reported to date.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Cases, such as this, remind us of the complexity of family relationships, and the crucial role that family and community intervention plays in helping vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The number of residents living alone is also projected to increase to more than 80,000 in 2030.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In our midst are vulnerable Singaporeans who may not be able to care for themselves, as they have physical or mental infirmities or disabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of these vulnerable individuals may not be able to depend on their families to provide adequate care for them; others may not even have family members or friends to rely on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While our adult protection framework has functioned well, there are instances where family and community interventions may not be effective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our experience, validated by feedback from our stakeholders, indicates that family matters are never clear-cut, never black and white.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Caregivers who abuse vulnerable adults may themselves be victims of difficult circumstances and be under tremendous stress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are sometimes unable to control their emotions, which may cause them to hurt vulnerable adults or other family members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One of the cases where MSF had to intervene involves “Sam”, again not his real name.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sam is a 29-year-old young man with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), autism and an intellectual disability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sam is an only child and lived with his elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, his parents were not able to understand his condition and, hence, care for Sam.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sam’s father would hit him to try and control his behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This resulted in severe cuts and bruises on Sam, all of which required medical attention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But Sam’s behaviour also caused his father a lot of stress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When MSF spoke with Sam’s family members, they mentioned that Sam’s father had entertained thoughts of killing his son and then ending his own life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sam’s father refused assistance and therapy for himself and his son, insisting that Sam be medicated to control his behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Given the high risk of Sam being hurt again, Sam was placed at a facility that was equipped to address his care needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In cases like this, the Government must take a proactive approach and intervene early, as any delays may lead to further harm, or worse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill will allow the Government social services to intervene, assist and protect vulnerable adults when social work-based family and community interventions are inadequate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It will complement other existing laws that protect vulnerable individuals, such as the Women’s Charter and the Mental Capacity Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we want to ensure that we have the ability to move quickly to protect and support vulnerable adults as well as their caregivers, when the need arises; and second, we want the protection for vulnerable adults to be effective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In drawing up the Bill, we consulted our community partners and public agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Together, we reviewed cases where vulnerable adults were abused, neglected or self-neglected themselves, and discussed how best to calibrate the powers that the Bill should give.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This was an important exercise that we did not want to rush, as we should not be excessively intruding into the sanctity of the home and eroding the autonomy and responsibility of the family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: During our consultations, we received strong support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I met our community partners earlier this year and the draft Bill was finalised, and I was encouraged by their continued strong support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have studied these views carefully and incorporated them into the Bill where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Before I go into the main provisions of the Bill, I would like to assure Members that the Bill does not and must not replace the social work that supports vulnerable adults and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is because personal care arrangements are largely matters for individuals and families to decide on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This Bill does not seek to supplant or diminish the role of the family and community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members can refer to the sheet that I passed around which gives a broad summary of the rest of my presentation, so I hope it is useful.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, four categories: first, the scope of the Bill and the guiding principles that underlie our intervention; second, MSF's ability to intervene and protect vulnerable adults; third, I will talk about Court orders that will enhance the protection and support for vulnerable adults and their caregivers; and, fourth, I will talk about community involvement in protecting vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will start with the first, which is the scope of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, the Bill protects vulnerable adults and explicitly sets out the guiding principles underlying state intervention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since its formation in 2015, MSF’s APS has seen a range of vulnerable adult cases involving abuse and neglect. “Abuse”, under the Vulnerable Adults Bill, refers to physical, emotional or psychological abuse. “Abuse” also includes any conduct or behaviour which causes an individual to fear for his safety or well-being, or unreasonably deprives, or threatens to unreasonably deprive, him of his liberty of movement or well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, an individual who excessively controls another individual’s day-to-day life and social relationships and, as a result, causes the individual to suffer adverse emotional health effects, may be regarded as having abused that individual.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A vulnerable adult may also require protection if he has been neglected. “Neglect” refers to the lack of provision of essential care to an individual, to the extent of causing or being reasonably likely to cause injury or pain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Not providing food, clothing, medical aid, lodging, supervision and other necessities of life are examples of neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A vulnerable adult may also neglect himself. “Self-neglect” refers to the failure of an individual to perform essential tasks of daily living, such as eating, drinking and seeking medical aid.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Vulnerable adults may, as a result of self-neglect, live in grossly unsanitary or hazardous conditions, suffer from malnutrition or dehydration, or suffer from untreated physical or mental illness or injury.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many do not have families to care for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Wong, again, not his real name, is an 85-year-old elderly man who lives alone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He has diabetes and has developed diabetic-related wounds on his feet.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When community workers found him, he had not bathed for months.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He did not keep his medical appointments despite running out of medication and was not able to take care of the wounds on his feet.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a result, maggots had infested the wounds on his leg and he required urgent hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But despite repeated engagements by community workers and by our social workers, Mr Wong refused to be admitted to a nursing home or a hospital.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Together, they persuaded him to accept medical care in his home, after getting assurances that his leg would not be amputated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: APS also managed to get help for Mr Wong to manage his swollen legs and to monitor his condition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As of today, nursing staff from a social service agency visit Mr Wong weekly to clean his wound and this has reduced the stench of rotting flesh from his right leg.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Each week, staff from our Senior Activity Centre visit him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They also arrange for a doctor to see him whenever necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Wong’s step-daughter also plays her part, dividing her time between work, her own family and children, and looking after Mr Wong.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are supporting her with caregiver support to help her cope.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When drafting the proposed definitions, we wanted to ensure that the Bill complements, but does not supplant, existing laws and support networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, an individual who is physically abused by a family member, but who is capable of protecting himself – in other words, he does not meet the vulnerability threshold under the Bill – may instead apply for a personal protection order (PPO) under the Women’s Charter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Individuals with suspected mental illness, who are not vulnerable adults, may also be assisted under the Mental Health Care and Treatment Act (MHCTA), if their behaviour places them at risk of harm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, clause 4 of the Bill sets out the five key principles that guide how we will exercise and carry out the duties or exercise the powers under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The powers of the Bill are intrusive into the family and, hence, must be exercised within limits and with the right intent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have, therefore, embedded these key principles in the Bill, to balance the need to protect a vulnerable adult with his right to autonomy and self-determination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, when we exercise the powers or perform the duties under the Bill, it must be to protect vulnerable adults from abuse, neglect and self-neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill is not intended to solve community disputes, nor remove persons from their homes just because they may be perceived by their family members or by neighbours to be a nuisance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will intervene if we assess that doing so is the only way to protect the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we recognise that a vulnerable adult with mental capacity is generally best placed to decide how he wishes to live, and whether or not to accept any assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill does not seek to override an individual’s freedom of choice nor coerce individuals to behave in a certain manner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF will seek an individual’s consent before intervening.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, there may be circumstances where we should intervene, even though the vulnerable adult has mental capacity and refuses to accept protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Such intervention will only take place in extreme cases involving the safety and protection of the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, we must consider the previously expressed views, wishes, feelings, values and beliefs of a vulnerable adult who lacks mental capacity, where reasonably ascertainable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF will, as far as possible, respect an individual’s choices and beliefs when we intervene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fourth, we must intervene and assist in a manner that is less restrictive of the vulnerable adult’s rights and freedom of action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In order to do this, MSF will work closely with the vulnerable adult and involve his family and caregivers, where possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fifth, the welfare and best interests of the vulnerable adult must be the paramount and first consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The next category of provisions sets out the state’s powers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Cases, such as Mr Wong, which I referred to earlier, illustrate why it is crucial for MSF to have powers to enter private premises, assess and, if necessary, remove a vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In severe cases, the vulnerable adult may no longer be safe within his place of residence or home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This allows swift assistance to be rendered to the vulnerable adult while other care arrangements are worked out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This requirement was included because we recognise that placement can significantly impact the vulnerable adult’s way of life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I wish to assure Members that committals to these care facilities will only be done as a last resort, for an appropriate duration, until the vulnerable adult can be safely reunited with his family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To ensure the vulnerable adult’s well-being and safeguard his health, MSF may require him to be treated by a registered medical practitioner or registered dentist before or during his stay in these care facilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Once committed to a care facility, the vulnerable adults must be protected from further harm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, clause 19 requires the care facilities to undertake security measures to ensure the safety and protection of the vulnerable adults residing within their premises, while clause 20 empowers MSF to establish a Review Board to ensure that proper care plans are in place for the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Review Board will also advise MSF on whether a vulnerable adult can be discharged when the period of committal ends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By and large, the Bill is premised on the vulnerable adult’s autonomy to make his own decisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That said, our experience working with vulnerable adults is that there are exceptional circumstances where we may have to intervene to ensure his safety despite his refusal to consent to intervention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes instances where the vulnerable adult refuses to consent to assistance because he is under duress or undue influence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, during our consultations, some stakeholders highlighted actual cases where they were unable to help a vulnerable adult, because he refused to accept their assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of these adults were abused or neglected until the day they died.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we looked at other countries which have longer experience with vulnerable adult legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of these jurisdictions have laws that allow a vulnerable adult’s stated wishes to be overridden.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in Scotland, the Adult Support and Protection Act permits the state to intervene despite a vulnerable adult’s refusal to consent, if there is evidence that the adult is unduly pressurised, and there are no other reasonable steps that can be taken to prevent further harm to that adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Similarly, in British Columbia, Canada, the state can intervene, without the vulnerable adult’s agreement, to remove an adult, provide them with emergency health care and take any other emergency measures necessary to protect the adult, if the adult is suffering from abuse or neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The state can do this if it is of the view that it is necessary to act without delay, in order to preserve the life of the adult; prevent serious physical or mental harm to the adult; or protect the adult’s property from significant damage or loss.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Like the adult protection laws in these countries, our Bill will similarly allow MSF to intervene despite a vulnerable adult’s wishes, if it is necessary to protect him and ensure his safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, as a safeguard, we will get a Court order to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ensuring the vulnerable adult's welfare and best interests is paramount.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, we must also hold abusers accountable for their actions if they are culpable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This aligns with the enhanced penalties for Penal Code offences against domestic workers who are also a vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Clause 42 also amends the Women's Charter to enhance the penalties for breaches of the Women's Charter, Personal Protection Orders (PPOs), to maintain parity with the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will now move on to the orders that the Court may make to protect vulnerable adults and support their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The need to apply for a Court order serves as a safeguard against excessive statutory intervention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When considering whether to make orders and what orders to make, the Court must have regard to the same five principles in the Bill that I have articulated earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it may also take into account any other relevant matters it deems fit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These Core Protection Orders protect the vulnerable adult from any third party who may cause him to suffer from abuse or neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It includes Restraining Orders, Exclusive Occupation Orders, and orders prohibiting a person from visiting or communicating with the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, Alternative Placement Supervision Orders, and what are these?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These orders ensure that the vulnerable adult is relocated to a safe environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Court may order a vulnerable adult to be committed to a care facility for a specified period of time, or order that the vulnerable adult be placed under the supervision of an appointed person.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This appointed person may include a protector or an approved welfare officer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, the Court can also make other protection and intervention orders, including orders to make the vulnerable adult's residence a safe living environment, and an order requiring the vulnerable adult or any other person to attend counselling or any such programmes as directed by the Court.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes the power to order a vulnerable adult or any other person, including a caregiver who may have caused the abuse or neglect to go for counselling or training and get additional support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some vulnerable adults may face difficulties applying for such Court orders on their own.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, clause 12 allows approved welfare officers to apply for Core Protection Orders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: More importantly, clause 12 preserves the role of the family as it also empowers family members, including a vulnerable adult's donee or deputy, to apply for protection orders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By donee, I refer to a person who has been appointed by the vulnerable adult under a Lasting Power Attorney (LPA) to make decisions on his behalf for his personal welfare, property and financial affairs, if and when he loses mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And by deputy, I refer to a person appointed by the Court to make such decisions on the vulnerable adult's behalf if he no longer has mental capacity to decide for himself and did not make an LPA earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our aim is to help every vulnerable adult to turn to the love and care of his family eventually.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I would like to come back and talk about Sam, that 29-year-old young man whose father had hit him in order to control his behaviour.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having Sam temporarily away from his home may also provide respite for Sam's parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF can then continue to engage Sam's father and ask that he attend therapy and counselling sessions to help him better understand and care for Sam and, if he refuses, we can try to apply to Court for an order requiring him to go for such counselling or other such programmes that the Court deems necessary as an added push.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill allows us to calibrate the level of intervention necessary for each case, through a combination of statutory orders as well as social work interventions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This complements our existing adult protection system which seeks to support both the vulnerable adult as well as their family and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members will recall the sad and tragic case of Ms Annie Ee.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Ee was a 26-year-old intellectually disabled waitress who left home because she wanted to work and be independent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She stayed with people whom she believed were her friends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Unfortunately, she was severely abused by her flat mates and eventually passed away.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While the Bill will allow the state to step in to protect individuals like Ms Ee, none of the intervention powers in this Bill will be meaningful unless those who meet and interact or come across vulnerable individuals like Ms Ee step forward and raise the alarm bells for community agencies and the authorities to intervene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in the case of Mdm Chua, in the first example I gave, her neighbours saw bruises on her arm and around her eyes and promptly sounded the alert.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our FSCs were, therefore, able to enquire about the circumstances and alert us to take action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have, therefore, included clauses in the Bill to strengthen the roles of both the family and community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These whistleblowers will be protected from civil and criminal liability, as long as they had acted with reasonable care and in good faith.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They will also not be regarded to have breached any professional etiquette or ethics.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will protect professionals, such as doctors, counselors, lawyers and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Any information that may lead to the identification of a vulnerable adult cannot be published or broadcast.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This would include MSF's community partners, such as our Family Violence Specialist Centres (FVSCs) and FSCs, as well as medical and healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is to ensure that swift action can be taken by different agencies to protect the vulnerable adult, hold perpetrators accountable, and ensure that appropriate assistance is provided to their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF recognises that working with vulnerable adults sometimes requires submitting of difficult professional judgements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Such protection is extended to any member of the Review Board, any person appointed by Court, and any person working in the care facilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, protection will only be afforded if they act professionally and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: (In Mandarin):  : Our population is ageing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By 2030, about one in four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As our demography changes and more individuals, along with their caregivers, age, more may face abuse, neglect and self-neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Vulnerable Adults Bill will better protect vulnerable adults living in our midst.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under the law, when caregivers did not take good care of the vulnerable adult in their family, the relevant authorities will have the power to intervene by appointing suitable family members to care for the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Family members may also apply for Court orders to prevent a perpetrator from having access to the vulnerable adult for his safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Individuals will be protected from legal liability, when they whistleblow and report alleged harm caused to a vulnerable adult or perform their duties to help a vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Such protection is given to anyone in the community who has acted in good faith, including professionals, family members, neighbours and members of the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Only where necessary, MSF will intervene to protect vulnerable adults, as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where family and community intervention has failed, MSF may enter a vulnerable adult's premises, assess his condition and relocate him for his safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To deter abuse and neglect, the law provides for heavier penalties for offences committed against vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to tell those caregivers who face challenges that you are not alone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Partners in the community, such as FSCs, stand ready to support you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Based on your family’s needs, they may provide counselling and support and, if required, link your family with agencies like the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) or SG Enable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There, your family members may benefit from care services for vulnerable seniors or persons with disabilities, such as day care or residential services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those of you who are caregivers may also receive respite care services so that you may take a break from your caregiving duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In order to care for our loved ones, we must also exercise self-care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Let us not wait until we are distressed and unintentionally harm those whom we love.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While helping others, do reach out to seek help early if you yourself need help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the Bill will only be effective if each and every one of us in the community continues to play our part.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We must look out for the safety of vulnerable people and extend warmth and a helping hand to families who care for their vulnerable family members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But the abuse and neglect of vulnerable adults are not a private matter and must not be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Everyone, including family members, neighbours, community leaders, employers and healthcare professionals, have a role to play to prevent vulnerable people from being abused, and to stop it if it happens.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let us step forward to break the silence by reporting suspected cases of abuse, neglect and self-neglect.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The comprehensiveness of the Bill is testament to the diligent and good work put in by the MSF team.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My work with some of the vulnerable adults reminds me of the usefulness of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have an elderly resident, a second-hand goods seller who hoards his entire rental flat and corridor with goods that he picks up in trolleys that he took from the nearby supermarkets.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With the flat completely filled with old goods, he sleeps instead at the void deck or the staircase nearby and incurred the resentment and wrath of his neighbours.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: His hygiene and daily living habits become a great concern to the people around him.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He refuses help except for the money he receives from passers-by who thought he was begging.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And his social worker and his only nephew are at their wits' end.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have another resident who suffers from mental illness, with violent tendencies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Her husband refuses to send her for treatment or supervise her well-being.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Neighbours who were physically threatened by her could not get assistance by the Police who claim there is nothing they can do until the neighbours get physically hurt first.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will practitioners on the ground or even members of the public learn, understand and interpret and apply the various provisions to assist persons who are vulnerable?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second is on balancing the state's right to enforce versus the citizen's right to choose.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill, in general, accords power to the Ministry which then appoints a director or protector, as stated in Part 2 of the Bill, such that the state can exercise the power to assess, enter premises, obtain information, remove and commit the vulnerable adult to a place of care and protection, sometimes against his will, if the state so decides.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mental incapacity falls upon a continuum of severity from mild to moderate to severe.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And there are also varying degrees of abuse, neglect by another person, or even self-neglect, which are all criteria applied in identifying a vulnerable adult in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, in the case of the elderly second-hand goods dealer I shared earlier, who appears not to have totally lost his mental capacity and yet showed serious signs of self-neglect, I am interested to know the course of action that the Ministry would undertake to support him.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How does the Bill balance the tension between state enforcement and a citizen's right of choice under such circumstances?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My third area of seeking clarification is on placement decision.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the event that a vulnerable adult is removed and placed in the gazetted care facility, what measures are taken by the Ministry to ensure that that these places of abode are suitable, dignified and staffed by persons who are properly trained to handle, especially the vulnerable elderly and/or the very severely disabled, some of whom would need specialised and expert care?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a small number – those who are supported in this way – compared to the universe of, I am sure, a much larger pool of adults who are potentially vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, are there any robust ongoing strategies to engage and equip the community, including neighbours, grassroots leaders, medical, social, Police and disability groups, so that suspect vulnerable adults in their midst are identified and supported earlier and not till damage is done either to themselves or others?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Without strong community support, many of these adults would fall through the cracks and remain unidentified until something tragic happens.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, legislation is, hence, only a small part of the solution.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To this end, Sir, I recommend that the Ministry seriously consider the formation of a National Vulnerable Adults Support Services Association, similar to that started elsewhere in the world, such as the US.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The association should aim to help organise, educate and train local residents and partners, community partners on the ground, to identify and support vulnerable adults in each private or public residential zone in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It can form local care groups, much like the cell groups that we commonly find in Christian or Buddhist organisations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It can play the role of an integrator, a social service integrator, to provide a tighter coordination of the many diverse voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) specialising in disabilities, elderly and mental health support organisations, FSCs, Residents' Committees (RCs) and other security and social support agencies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The association can also look at providing scalable upstream and downstream services to meet the diverse needs of the ever-changing and enlarging population of vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With such an association, many more adults with varying degrees of vulnerability would be able to then receive the needed support upstream in their neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: John, not his real name, was a young man who had severe autism.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He was living with his very protective mother who also had special needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mom, his sole caregiver, rejected treatment for John, sometimes refusing to send him to school when he was younger.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mom was also very insistent on doing things her way, often verbally abusing and avoiding the agency staff who tried to assist.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We wept when we paid respects at his funeral wake.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another man I know with a developmental disability had a better fate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He is a resident whom I found during my house-to-house visits as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Er Ge, as he is now fondly known, was locked up in his rental flat as well whilst his elder brother went to work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Fearing for his safety and well-being, my grassroots and I approached the nearby PeaceConnect Senior Activity Centre.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, Er Ge has a whole community supporting him in a day centre and a very vibrant social life at least, compared to me.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, Sir, with that, I fully support the Bill and thank the Ministry for this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even as our intentions are noble, our perception of what is in the vulnerable adult's best interest may not accord with theirs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a Bible passage that literally captures the powerlessness that older people feel as they become more dependent on others.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Acts of the Apostles, Jesus is recorded as saying to his disciple Peter: "When you were younger, you used to dress yourself and go where you wanted, but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, I endorse the fundamental principles set out in clause 4 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I support the rationale for the Bill, there are a few aspects of the Bill that concern me, which I shall summarise as follows.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I raise these issues so that the Ministry can clarify, in order to have greater public understanding of how the Bill will operate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, I will touch on some areas that need further attention to enable vulnerable adults to live fuller lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, division of work under the Bill and the Office of Public Guardian.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the Mental Capacity Act, the Public Guardian's Office was set up to perform certain functions vis-à-vis mentally impaired persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These functions include supervising the way donees and deputies perform their duties under Lasting Powers of Attorney and Court Orders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Public Guardian is tasked with looking into complaints about donees or deputies who do not act in the person's best interest, either in managing his personal welfare or his property and affairs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When this Bill is in place, there will be some overlap when it comes to a vulnerable adult's personal welfare.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I assume that this Bill will tackle the cases where there is no donee or deputy appointed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the Bill also covers cases where there are donees and deputies, as seen, for example, in clause 6.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The question then arises: should there be a case involving donees or deputies that requires state intervention, to whom should a complaint be made?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it to the Director of Social Welfare under this Bill, or to the Public Guardian under the Mental Capacity Act, or can both be pursued concurrently?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, the Bill does not cover abuse of a vulnerable adult's financial assets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Where there are donees or deputies appointed, a complaint can be made to the Public Guardian that the donee or deputy has acted in bad faith.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But if there is no donee or deputy, the Ministry has stated that the Police would investigate any criminal offences reported.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the criminal justice system is geared towards punishment, how does one undo or reverse financial transactions, so as to restore monies or properties to the vulnerable adult?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One can always apply to Court if one has the means.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But what if a person does not have the means or does not have any family member to do so?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second point is about the rigour of assessment and the risk of Government overreach.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In discussing this area, my concern is about mentally impaired persons and the state's power to remove a vulnerable adult from his current residence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The state can do this if the person is assessed to be suffering from abuse, neglect or self-neglect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe that the Government would not wish to be over-zealous in exercising such powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, in the Second Reading speech, the Minister did reaffirm that social work interventions would basically need to be exhausted first before the Bill will be triggered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, excessive intervention will harm the vulnerable adults and also be an unreasonable burden on public resources.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the state's power under the Bill is correctly limited.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to clause 4, a vulnerable adult's views must be respected if he is able to make his views known.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 4(b) states that where he has mental capacity, he is generally best placed to decide how he or she wishes to live and whether or not to accept any assistance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even where he lacks mental capacity, clause 4(c) makes it clear that his views, whether past or present, wishes, feelings, values and beliefs, where reasonable ascertainable, must be considered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my personal experience with family members and constituents with dementia, dementia is not a static condition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are good days and bad days, with moments of lucidity when the person seems to think normally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Dementia patients may speak clearly at times, but do they always understand the implications of the wishes they are expressing?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Being institutionalised generally comes with a loss of pride and a loss of autonomy, having to live by an institution's rules.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Dementia patients can be very agitated and difficult to handle in unfamiliar environments or when surrounded by strangers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Moving such a person from his home to an institution would likely be very damaging to the person's psychological and emotional well-being.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What rigour of assessment will be used before such drastic intervention will be triggered?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What standard of care do we expect from caregivers when they care for vulnerable adults?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We usually see caregivers being spouses or children, who love their family members deeply.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, caring for dementia sufferers is onerous, exhausting and physically risky.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Caregivers may also have other obligations, such as work or caring for other family members.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And earlier, I think the Minister gave an example of a Mdm Chua and I think her family fits this description which I have just made.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such caregivers are often not medical or healthcare professionals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By what yardstick will they be assessed if a complaint is made?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, there are somewhat wide definitions in the Bill about what amounts to abuse, neglect and self-neglect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, if a caregiver decides not to bring the person out because she cannot manage him in public, is that an unreasonable deprivation of liberty?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for being unreasonably deprived of well-being, the illustrations in clause 2 also need closer scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It states that if a caregiver does not dress the adult after bathing her and leaves her unclothed in a room with windows open that can be seen by neighbours, that amounts to depriving a person of her personal dignity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the modesty of the individual certainly needs respect, there could be valid reasons why the caregiver left the adult as such after a bath.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, it could be that the caregiver needed some time to prepare medicines that need to be applied on the person's body.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, the caregiver needed to attend to an urgent phone call or other task.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It speaks of a caregiver who refuses to allow a vulnerable adult to receive visitors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But what if the caregiver did so because the adult had reacted badly to visitors in the past, shouting at them and even pushing them away?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What if the visitors are young children, who might be traumatised to witness such behaviour?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, does the Bill risk inadvertent discrimination against the poor?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will the definitions of "abuse", "neglect" and "self-neglect" impact poor families or individuals?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, we sometimes see multigeneration families living in small rental flats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will a vulnerable adult sleeping on a mattress without a proper bed be considered "neglected"?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What if the vulnerable adult would benefit from certain treatment which requires payment, but he does not have the means to pay for it?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, there are psychiatric drugs to treat aggression, but some of these drugs are not subsidised and are costly, especially when prescribed long term.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the vulnerable adult be considered neglected if the family cannot afford such treatment?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not saying that the Bill intends to discriminate against the poor, but could this be an inadvertent result?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has been increasingly active in addressing issues, such as ageing and mental health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the Government has enabled parents of disabled children to access a simplified, low-cost procedure to be appointed as deputies when their children reach adulthood.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another scenario I have come across is that of adults who lose their mental capacity later in life and have modest bank balances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From time to time, they also receive some top-ups from the Government, which go into their bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Because of their lack of capacity, they are unable to sign documents and family members are unable to access those monies for their medical treatment or upkeep.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My next point is about increasing the social space for vulnerable adults to engage in public activities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the case of mental impairment, however, there is less public understanding of the condition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Families with dementia sufferers tend to limit their social lives, due to the discomfort caused in public by the odd behaviour of their family members.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an area that we can all continue to work on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With greater public understanding of dementia and its manifestations, society can show kindness and support towards families and individuals stricken with mental illness and be more welcoming and understanding towards such families.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Public education efforts can be stepped up to increase awareness of conditions like dementia, and I agree with the Minister that all of us can play a part in this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The institutions involved could make life more bearable by little gestures to preserve the person's individual identity and autonomy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, instead of requiring residents to wear a uniform, could they be allowed to don their own clothing?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could residents be encouraged to have a space to place family photographs and other effects from home?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These seemingly small gestures will go a long way to reassure the individual in an unfamiliar institutional environment.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone has the right to live in safety, free from neglect, abuse, free from fear and coercion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is so, whether the person is powerful or vulnerable, or has or does not have mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill has been a long time coming, and I am glad it has finally come.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is a good start, but I am sure the Minister will agree with me that there will be more to be done to protect vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill has been a long time coming because it touches on sensitive matters – a person's right to live where he chooses; a person's right to be cared for; a family's right to care for a vulnerable adult.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But when we enter into sensitive family spaces, we can expect to deal with deep-seated family tensions and grievances, strong and overwhelming family dynamics, family reputation; strong ties of love, loyalty, kinship and obligation, feelings of guilt, resentment, contempt, financial challenges, emotional and relational dysfunction, misguided action or inaction.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And, very often, many, if not all, in one set of relationships.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, understandably, the Government does not want to be interventionist.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And, understandably, my hon colleague, Ms Sylvia Lim, also cautioned quite wisely against a judicious exercise of power.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And yet, we need to strike a balance -- a balance against the right of another person to act, as opposed to the need to protect the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And this balance must be prudent and yet bold, and it must be struck in favour of protecting the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I may share that this may well be a difference in perspectives.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: A few years ago, someone shared with me from the social service sector that in the earlier years, when there were voices calling for transport concessions, there were people in the social service sector serving people with disabilities who opposed those voices.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In their view, it was the dignity of people with disabilities that mattered more, that, by virtue of upholding that dignity, we should not concede and ask for transport concessions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Strangely, the person then shared that when the Government announced these policies, and they consulted people with disabilities, the people with disabilities said they wanted it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, it just could be a matter of perspective.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We could be professionals and we could be very well-meaning and say we want to preserve your dignity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But if I am a vulnerable person, maybe, I want more to be protected.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: By this, I suppose a balance and an assessment that the Government and the professionals have to assess, have to make.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But again, I urge it must be struck in favour of protecting the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When a "stranger" enters into any family space, he or she will be confronted with the question: "who are you?" What it really means, in our context, is: "what right have you to interfere in my family matters?" What right do you have?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, social workers, support service providers and Government offices, while actively engaged on the ground to assist and support vulnerable adults and their families, are hampered in their attempts to protect such adults – not much right.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not much that can be done and, hence, we welcome this Bill.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Nobody in our right mind or heart will ask, "what right have you to protect the vulnerable adults?" But we should not, indeed, be surprised that family members will demand, "what right have you to interfere in my family matters?" And that is, in fact, a fair question, and that is a question that must be answered by this House now, unequivocally.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We must answer this question clearly and unequivocally by, firstly, setting out clearly the scope of the protection for vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Anyone whose circumstances do not fall within the scope of production, will not be able to claim such protection.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think it has got to be clear in our minds that we must have a Bill that is broad enough to protect.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The protection must be sufficiently significant to an adult.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And thirdly, persuading the community that each person has a role to play in the protection of vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These three questions we must answer unequivocally today.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Both issues relate to the scope of protection, and I will share my views as to what I think the limitations in certain definitions are and state my proposals for amendments.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the interest of time, however, I will not repeat the definitions word for word, and I seek the indulgence of hon Members to refer to the Bill as I speak.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I have to admit I am not comfortable with the word "mean" or "means" in that definition.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It limits the definition as opposed to the word "includes".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Again, the word "means", is very limiting, as opposed to "include".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Also, it means the failure of an individual to perform essential tasks of daily living to care for himself, resulting in the individual suffering certain prescribed consequences or conditions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This amendment broadens the scope of protection and empowers the Director with clarity, confidence and courage in the exercise of his powers to protect vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: With reference to the definition of "self-neglect", there are also other limitations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: At least one of the three must occur before the Director can intervene.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, the Director cannot intervene to protect the individual until something extremely terrible has happened.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: That should not and cannot be the intention of the Minister.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Certainly, it should not be condoned or be the intention of this House.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Director should have the power to intervene if the failure to care for oneself could reasonably be expected to cause any of those three consequences.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is bad enough to live in unsanitary or hazardous conditions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should not require such living conditions to be gross in order to justify intervention.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The deletion of the word "grossly" will also remove ambiguity as to whether “grossly” qualifies only "unsanitary" or qualifies "hazardous" as well.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The narrower the definitions, the narrower the scope of protection.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Minister and this House to consider my proposals.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I now move on to three aspects of the protection.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: However, again, the definition of "assessment" seems somewhat limited to me.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not clear as to whether psychological assessments are included.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister can clarify.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If, indeed, "assessment" does not include psychological assessments, then I urge the Minister to consider amending the definition to include the same.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding that there may be many non-legal triggers for the protection of a vulnerable adult, assessment itself is an important trigger.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond re-examining the definition of "assessment", we should also re-examine the requirement for a Court order where a vulnerable adult, notwithstanding his or her mental capacity, refuses, under coercion, to give consent for his or her removal for such assessment.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For the ease of recollection by Members, section 10 empowers the Director to remove a vulnerable adult from the place where the vulnerable adult is residing or staying if the Director is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the vulnerable adult has experienced, or is experiencing or is at risk of, abuse, neglect or self-neglect.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Two important considerations from the basis of my submissions on the inadequacies of section 6 and section 10.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: One, where the individual or vulnerable adult does not give consent, but is also not acting freely, for example, where he or she refuses consent for fear of reprisals from or unhappiness of caregivers or of family members.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Under the Bill, mental capacity is used in the same sense as under the Mental Capacity Act.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This leaves a large group of persons who may have inadequate reasoning faculties, but who may not lack mental capacity under the Mental Capacity Act, for example, those with low intelligence or suffering from certain spectrum of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), or in the early stages of dementia.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In both groups, the lack of financial independence, lack of social support network, and emotional attachment to familiar people, the Stockholm syndrome, may increase their dependency on their family members or increase their fear in reporting.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We know that it is common for caregivers who refuse medical assessment.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is a problem that we need to address.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot assume that these two groups of people do not require protection simply because they have refused to give consent.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I support the provisions, in fact, that the Director may, without the consent of the relevant donee or deputy, assess a vulnerable adult without mental capacity, recognising that some donees or deputies are themselves abusers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But, here, the two groups of persons whom I referred to above are no less vulnerable than those who lack mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, they could be more vulnerable simply because they have the capacity to consent.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And should they give consent or should they in any way intimate fear or convey simply a need for protection, they are more likely to be held to account by their abusers, caregivers and family members.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The fear of the vulnerable adult is thereby accentuated.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have noted that the Bill provides for the Director to make an application to the Court for the vulnerable adult to be removed, whether for an assessment under section 6, or for removal under section 10.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I submit that the Director should be given broader powers than to be constrained in this manner.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: My reasons follow from my analysis as to how a Court order may be obtained for the assessment of an individual or a vulnerable adult.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In a Court application, first, the Director must make the application to the Court.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Any concern as to whether the Director may be acting too intrusively may be addressed by amending section 11(1)(b) as well as related provisions accordingly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I may, I would also like to share an additional concern in relation to the removal of the vulnerable adult for assessment.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, the Director may also choose not to make an application to Court.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: If I may also add, the role of the community cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill is a welcomed piece of legislation to protect some of the most vulnerable in society but also raises difficult questions of the role the state should play in intervening in the most intimate of relationships, and in interfering with decisions and preferences of an adult on matters of their own care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The long period of gestation for the Bill reflects the delicate process of balancing protection and respect for individual autonomy and freedom.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I stand in support of the Bill and the principles set out under section 4, which articulates the restraint and proportionality that should guide the exercise of the extensive powers under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have a few points of clarification on the scope of protection offered by the Bill, the mechanisms for checks on the exercise of powers, and measures for protecting vulnerable adults beyond those set out under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point really is what I started this speech with.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why did it take so long to introduce this Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What were the various considerations or challenges MSF faced in introducing this important Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, under the Bill, a vulnerable adult is defined as an individual who is 18 or older.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the rationale for setting 18 years old as the lower age limit for a vulnerable adult?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Children and Young Persons Act protects individuals who are under 16.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the forms of equivalent legal protection and recourse available to those who are between 16 and 18?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, sexual abuse is not listed as a type of abuse under section 2(1).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, "physical abuse" is defined to include coercion or attempts at coercing an individual to engage in sexual activity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This definition of sexual abuse as being a subset of physical abuse is too narrow because not all sexual harassment is physical.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, vulnerable adults may be subject to verbal sexual harassment not amounting to coercion in engaging sexual activities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the rationale for subsuming sexual abuse under physical abuse, and also clarify how verbal sexual harassment will be dealt with under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, would the Minister consider introducing or including sexual abuse as an independent head of abuse?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, the definition of "abuse" under section 2(1) does not include financial abuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is also a lack of provisions in the Bill that address financial abuse of vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Financial abuse, such as financial exploitation, is a significant problem faced by vulnerable adults and is a form of elder abuse recognised by MSF.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The definition of ill-treatment under the Mental Capacity Act, which protects mentally incapacitated elders from ill-treatment by their caregiver or donee or deputy does not include financial abuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider extending the ambit of the Bill to protection against financial abuse in the future?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the current legal protections available to vulnerable adults subject to financial abuse?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Director and protectors have extensive discretion and powers under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Caregivers may legitimately worry about disruption and interference in their lives, such as the possibility of entry into their homes and premises.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Excessive intervention may also further strain relationships between elderly parents and their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These extensive state powers must thus be exercised with great restraint and proportionality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify what mechanisms exist for review and oversight of the powers granted to the Directors and protectors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister consider instituting a formal approval or reporting process for the most intrusive powers exercised by the Directors and protectors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would include the powers to remove an individual for assessment without consent, to enter premises, to remove a vulnerable adult from their place of residence and to require medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify the instances where the Director or protector need not seek a donee or deputy's consent before assessing or removing a vulnerable adult under section 6(2) and section 10(2)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that cases of abuse, neglect or self-neglect often occur outside the public eye, effectiveness of the Bill, as the Minister has mentioned, is contingent on detection and reporting of such cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will training be provided to frontline staff to sensitise them to indicators of abuse, neglect or self-neglect?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that Social Services Offices and other community partners can call MSF to report cases of vulnerable adult abuse, but vulnerable adults who are not in contact with community partners may fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister consider setting up a public hotline under the Adult Protective Services for reporting vulnerable adult abuse, as has been done with the MSF Child Protective Services Helpline?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can the Minister clarify the ways in which the Adult Protective Services are similar or different from the Child Protective Services?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Vulnerable Adults Bill is a timely and necessary creation to address the needs of a rapidly ageing population, and to bolster our existing legal frameworks.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have spoken much about bold ideas, but less about real action.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is an example of a small but significant change that we can make.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A change that is literally a matter of life and death for thousands of older Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The urgency and scale of the problem cannot be denied.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The law, as it currently stands, is inadequate insofar as the state lacks the authority to intervene.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, the state has been unable to enter the homes to render timely assistance to vulnerable adults who might be abused by their caregivers or are in a serious state of self-neglect, if the owner of the home refuses them permission to enter.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The case of Mdm Ee, a 79-year-old single woman who lives alone, shows us this in real life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She is mentally incapacitated – a schizophrenic – and she has no next-of-kin.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She rebuffs all attempts at treatment and intervention from healthcare professionals and social workers alike.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Meal delivery services were also ignored as Mdm E left delivered meals at her gate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, the risk of self-neglect is very high.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The mentally-ill elderly who live alone, such as Mdm E, are prone to untreated falls and illnesses and may not have ready access to food.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another case shows how timely this proposed Bill is.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mrs A, she is an 81-year-old woman suffering from dementia and is incapable of activities of daily living.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She was abused physically, emotionally and psychologically by her 87-year-old husband who himself is prone to violent outbursts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They used to stay together alone and away from their adult children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But their children's fear of the father made them unable to supervise the elderly couple, leaving Mrs A without any protective figures at home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The new Bill allows for such cases of self-neglect and abuse, which usually also involve uncooperative or non-communicative vulnerable adults, to be addressed efficiently, without the need for lengthy and unproductive negotiations with either the aggressor or the victim.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This Bill allows us to act pre-emptively to protect vulnerable adults against caregiver abuse and neglect, and victim self-neglect.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Stakeholders, such as medical and social workers, AIC, the Police and perhaps even finance professionals, could be legally obliged to report suspected abuse as long as they have reasonable grounds to believe that a vulnerable adult has been neglected or abused.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The underlying principle is that with a group of people as vulnerable as those considered here, those who are unable or unwilling to voice their pains, worries and concerns, it is wiser to be wrong than sorry; it is better, in my opinion, to err on the side of caution, because under-reporting of abuse is likely to be the norm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The difficulty, as is always the case, lies in the details – who is required to report?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Do we restrict the obligation to care professionals or should we include neighbours, friends and family members?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Should less-tangible forms of abuse, such as psychological and emotional abuse, be covered?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Would it be overly onerous to penalise the third party for non-reporting of such less tangible abuses?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What about financial abuse, which my fellow Parliamentarian Mr Louis Ng just talked about?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What sanctions will be imposed for failing to report, taking into account the bystander effect, that witnesses of abuse are more reluctant to shoulder the burden of reporting if there are other witnesses?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Lessons can perhaps be drawn from overseas jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Washington has a mandatory reporting requirement in cases of elder financial abuse, though relatives, friends and neighbours are exempted from this obligation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Likewise, the state of Illinois imposes an obligation to report on "includes employees of the state of Illinois who provide medical or rehabilitation services to adults, law enforcement officers and social service workers" to guard against elder financial abuse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More fundamentally, we must strike an acceptable balance between protection and intrusion into personal affairs, taking into account Singapore's cultural norm of non-interference.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is my view that the Bill, which already protects whistleblowers, can be tweaked to include mandatory reporting and yet protect these stakeholders from liability arising from provision of such information or breaches of any code of professional conduct.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Penalising the willfully blind heightens stakeholder awareness of their wards' vulnerabilities and improves oversight over the welfare of vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The social need for adequate protection of the most vulnerable amongst us charges us with a moral duty to find this balance, regardless of how difficult it is.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Fellow Parliamentarians, such as Dr Lily Neo and Mr Chia Yong Yong, and professors, such as Prof Chan Wing Cheong, and non-government organisations (NGOs), such as the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE), have repeatedly raised this concern.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And again, Mr Louis Ng just raised this as well.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But financial abuse can be as devastating as other forms of abuse and neglect.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They can also be precursors to physical abuse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As AWARE observes, financial abuse is "often accompanied by threats of physical violence, and compounds the vulnerability of a victim to further abuse and neglect".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Vulnerable adults, due to their physical or mental infirmities, are less able to safeguard their financial security, or may be held hostage by their live-in caregivers, or lack the financial resources to take civil action.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are well-aware of cases of over-trusting parents who part with their assets out of love for their children, children who subsequently forsake them, whether due to a lack of filial piety or disagreements in the family.
