speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Other cases include deceiving or coercing an elderly parent to sign a will or deed or taking money from them without providing support in return.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Furthermore, financial abuse is under-reported, due to its subtle, non-tangible nature.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The definitions used in other jurisdictions, such as in New York, Washington and Illinois, can potentially be transplanted with modifications.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some US states even go so far as to impose a mandatory reporting obligation on professionals who are aware of elder financial abuse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, this is not the first time that the financial interests of the vulnerable have been debated in this House.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Maintenance of Parents Act, passed in 1996 and amended in 2010, allows elderly parents who are unable to maintain themselves adequately to apply for an order to have their children sustain him or her financially.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Bill tabled before us today gives us the opportunity to act more pre-emptively; to treat the scourge of financial exploitation at its root.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Instead of ensuring that the vulnerable receives financial maintenance after the act of abuse has taken place, is it not more effective to remove the threat in the first place?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such pre-emptive action ensures that whatever financial resources that the vulnerable adult still possesses are not taken away by abusers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, who pays for the permanent care or relocating of the vulnerable adults?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Would it be from the vulnerable adult's Central Provident Fund, or the abuser or the Government?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think this point was raised by the National University of Singapore Centre for Biomedical Ethics, and I agree that some clarification would be good.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As is often said, a society is judged by how it treats its weakest members.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Bill, in combating the social ill of the abuse of vulnerable adults, not only meets the changing needs of Singaporeans – its ageing population, falling birth rates and elders who live alone – but also affirms the values of the Singapore that we all know and are proud of.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Vulnerable Adults Bill must recalibrate our traditional aversion to interventionistic laws, against the reality of the everyday lives of older Singaporeans on the ground.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It should not be an obstacle against protecting the highly vulnerable, whether they be children or adults, exceptions must be made where called for.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The welfare of vulnerable adults is one such instance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, there is broad support for this proposed law from the social services sector and the public, and I would like to echo the support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is an important instrument of last resort to be used to safeguard the well-being of vulnerable individuals facing abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I personally witnessed a case where multiple Government and social service agencies were scrambling to intervene to safeguard an elderly woman's well-being after community and family interventions have failed to rescue the mentally incapacitated lady from self-neglect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The crux of the problem was who had the power to compel the lady to accept assessment and assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It took years to finally get help to the lady in need which had, in the meantime, caused much distress to the family and the neighbours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have three points to raise about the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But before I raise these points, I would like to ask an important question of clarification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MSF first mooted the Vulnerable Adults Bill in 2014, and it was said that the Bill would likely be enacted in 2015.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That did not happen and the public consultation on the Bill took place in 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Almost two years have passed since and we are here at the Second Reading of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The frequently asked questions accompanying the public consultation documents for the Bill stressed that the rate of abuse of vulnerable adults is relatively low and that the Bill is important to keep this rate low as the Singapore society ages and the number of senior citizens increases to 900,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ageing society is also cited as the impetus for the Bill in the other documents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the ageing society is the crucial context, I believe the central motivation of the Bill should not be about keeping rates low as the society ages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should be about reducing abuse to the minimal and safeguarding vulnerable adults in all cases of abuse regardless of the societal context because one abuse is one too many and should be stopped.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, the motivation and the spirit of this law should be more humanistic and less bureaucratic in the sense of measuring abuse in terms of a key performance indicator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, this rate of three years for the Bill to be tabled needs to be accounted for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There must be a good reason or good reasons for the delay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister said we should not rush this Bill in his speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first point is about the definitions and the scope of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is very good that the principle in clause 4 states that, "In all matters relating to the administration or application of this Act, the welfare and best interest of the vulnerable adult must be the first and paramount consideration" has been added to the Bill after public consultation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It signals that the main motivation for the Bill is not about keeping abuse rates low, but in protecting the basic human dignity of the weakest members of our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there appears to be two gaps in the definition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A vulnerable adult is defined in the Bill as an individual aged 18 and above who is incapable of protecting himself from abuse, neglect or self-neglect due to physical or mental incapacity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that close to 200,000 individuals each year entering what is arguably a very emotionally volatile phase of growth as late teens would neither be protected under the Bill nor under the Children and Young Persons' Act, which defines young persons as under 16 years of age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While financial abuse is not as physically apparent as other forms, it is equally harmful to the vulnerable adult's well-being and best interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Feedback during the public consultation phase highlighted these two gaps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MSF responded to the feedback by implying that the two gaps are covered by other laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regarding older young persons, MSF stated that the Women's Charter provides protection for victims of family violence of all ages, and that there are many services and programmes on the ground catering to older youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the whole point of having the Bill is precisely to give MSF protectors the powers to intervene to stop the abuse when family and community interventions have failed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Women's Charter does not provide these important powers of last resort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be tragic if, because of this definition handicap, MSF protectors would have to wait for two years to intervene to rescue a young person aged 16 facing abuse by reason of physical or mental incapacity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, would the Minister consider amending the definition of vulnerable adults to lower the age to 16 years, or amending the Children and Young Persons Act to cover young persons who are up to 17 years of age?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regarding financial abuse, MSF stated that the Police can investigate financial offences under the Penal Code, and the Office of Public Guardian can apply to Court to suspend or revoke the powers of a vulnerable adult's donee or deputy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, financial abuse is much more insidious and hidden.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And it often involves elements of psychological and emotional abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, the whole point of having the Bill is to enable the MSF protectors to intervene to stop the abuse and harm caused to the vulnerable adults, which is something the Police and the Office of Public Guardian cannot do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I mean by this is that the MSF protectors should be allowed to exercise some powers of the Bill while family and community interventions are ongoing so that the latter – the family and community interventions – could be supported and enhanced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This pertains to the powers of getting information of the suspected vulnerable adults, entering private premises to assess well-being, and compelling vulnerable adults to receive medical or dental treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, these powers have to be assessed judiciously so as not to compromise family and community interventions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The power to remove and relocate the vulnerable adults should remain the power of last resort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister comment on how these powers would be operationalised and exercised vis-à-vis the family and community interventions on the ground?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, I would like to go back to the question of financial abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If, in the course of an investigation and ongoing family and community interventions, it is discovered that the vulnerable adult is facing financial abuse in having his or her resources exploited for the perpetrators personal benefit, what recourse does the MSF protector have to intervene to protect the vulnerable adult?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the MSF protector refer the case to the Police or the Office of Public Guardian?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is one more issue I would like to raise with regard to intermediate powers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is regarding situations where vulnerable adults face economic abuse in not having their needs being met because of the lack of financial support from family members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The power to remove and relocate the individual under the Bill may actually not be in the best interest of the vulnerable adult as she may benefit more in residing and receiving care in their own home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears that the intermediate power is needed here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not keen to suggest that the MSF protector be empowered to apply on behalf of the vulnerable adult for maintenance from his/her children under the Maintenance of Parents Act as I am instinctively wary of quipping state intrusion into the prerogatives of the family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what other intermediate recourse is available to MSF officers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third and last point I would like to raise about the Bill is the connection and potential overlap with the provisions in the Women's Charter catering to the protection of victims of family violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While this Bill appears to be motivated by the need to especially protect the vulnerable elderly from the risk of abuse in an ageing society, the definition of vulnerable adult is broad enough to encompass victims of family violence, particularly family violence of the most egregious kind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whilst spousal victims of family violence are most likely not in the first instance, be it the mentally or physically incapacitated, in many cases of egregious abuse, spousal victims, and most of them being women, become mentally incapacitated because of sustained abuse, and are incapable of protecting themselves from further abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If, in fact, it does, then I would like to ask the Minister what the division of labour and powers would be like in the provisions in the Women's Charter and in the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am asking this because there could be quite a lot of confusion on the ground after the enactment of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Social service agencies and concerned whistleblowers may choose to report incidents of family violence to MSF for more immediate intervention under the Bill instead of the more laborious route of helping victims to apply for Personal Protection Orders (PPOs) from the Court.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am personally in favour and open for spousal victims of family violence who have become mentally incapacitated by abuse to be deemed as vulnerable adults so that they can receive the needed assistance from MSF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, I am concerned that MSF resources could be stretched and overwhelmed if MSF officers have to investigate even a proportion of family violence cases to determine whether intervention under the Bill is warranted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The idea is to avoid concerned family members and friends of victims of spousal abuse expecting and going for the nuclear option of removing the victims from their homes unless it is absolutely necessary to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The conversations and debates should be welcomed and embraced because I think they will push us forward as a people grappling together with the issues of human vulnerability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill is timely and actually somewhat delayed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to put on record my thanks to the MSF officers who work very hard to not just care for the needy, but also proactively consult VWOs as we change the law.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Members from the VWO sector whom I spoke to are supportive of this amendment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It strengthens how we protect our seniors, especially during a crisis.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I especially appreciated the part about protecting whistleblowers because we do need our community to come in and tell the state when people most need help.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A collaboration between MSF and Silver Generation Office (SGO) can go far for us to stay in touch with vulnerable adults regularly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the Government has a database called the Developmental Disability Registry (DDR) to track our vulnerable adults and children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This database likely contains a large percentage of them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But it is possible that some of them are not captured in the database.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To improve on this matter, during regular SGO’s outreach to seniors, a small group of vetted and well-trained Silver Generation Ambassadors (SGAs) can be assigned to visit the vulnerable adults already in the registry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These SGAs can refer them to social workers, if necessary, and also update the registry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, when other SGAs chance upon any vulnerable adults or children in their outreach session, they can also include that information into the registry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SGO’s involvement will go very far to help us in the know about every vulnerable adult or children in Singapore and, in doing so, can potentially forestall some of the tragedies involving vulnerable adults later on.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I will speak about getting Singaporeans to do up their LPAs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With our ageing population, there will many more adults who, through illnesses or accidents over their lives, grow dependent on their family and friends.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If these adults get mentally incapacitated, their caregivers could have difficulties mobilising enough resources to help them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Without a strong support network, some of these mentally incapacitated Singaporeans will become vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We should tackle the problem upstream, by encouraging all Singaporeans to create LPAs, which identify and authorise a "donee" to act on his/her behalf, including on financial matters, when he/she is mentally incapacitated.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Should no LPA exist after mental incapacity sets in, there are still options to deal with it, but it gets complicated.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Family members and friends can apply to be Court-appointed deputies, which is time-consuming and costly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MSF's new Community Kinship Service pilot can get social workers to be Court-appointed deputies and, therefore, take charge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But most of us here in this Chamber would agree that MSF's limited resources should focus on only the most pressing of cases.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, to minimise the number of vulnerable adults ahead of the coming Silver Tsunami, LPAs play a major part.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I have assembled a team of lawyers and community leaders to think about this issue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We believe a major LPA adoption drive is necessary and would like to propose three steps.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, integrate the LPA into relevant Government processes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This will give many Singaporeans the chance to think through this issue and make a decision and draw up their LPAs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Housing and Development Board (HDB) can insert the LPA process within all deed transfers and name insertions for people above 55.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MOH can get hospitals to advise moderate to high-risk and senior patients to get LPAs and offer that process in major hospitals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, we can minimise the cost of LPAs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The current cost is not costly, but to get mass adoption of LPAs by seniors and retirees, we can try to bring down the cost even more.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MSF can extend the waiver of LPA application cost.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At pre-selected Government offices issuing large numbers of LPA certifications, we can include an onsite team of certifiers, that is, lawyers, doctors and psychiatrists.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And the benefit of this is that we can then offer out bulk-contracts for these certification services to further reduce the cost from lawyers, doctors and psychiatrists.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Another option is for us to train civil servants who know about these issues to act as certifiers at key locations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our third point is that we need to communicate extensively.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can explain about LPAs through videos in different languages.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These videos can be made and screened on television, within cinema and online.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SGO can explain the importance of LPAs to seniors, and we can also communicate the importance through various community health screenings.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure a big push will increase the LPA numbers and we must monitor the adoption very carefully.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, if the situation does not improve within a few years, I hope we can consider even more decisive steps.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Talking to my team of lawyers and community leaders, the tricky part of the default LPA option is how the law should determine the donees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The most obvious way the law can determine the donee is to use the succession rules from the Inter-Succession Act.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But even if we go down that path, we need to consider whether the default donee should be an individual, or a group of natural heirs with collective responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And if there are collective responsibilities, how should responsibilities be divided up, and how do we reconcile the difference in views and motivations among the natural heirs in the process?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we go down the path of default LPAs, it would also be good for us to clarify the powers of donees with regard to utilising the assets of the donors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To conclude, I warmly welcome and support the amendments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With stronger laws in place, I hope we can improve how we care for our vulnerable seniors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Such individuals may include the elderly, as well as persons with disability and special needs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is about time that the Vulnerable Adults Bill is set to complement existing laws that address violence, maltreatment and abuse against vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On empowering state intervention, I have the following four questions.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Two, how do we first establish early identification of this group of vulnerable adults?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Three, how can MSF take on a more active than reactive role when it comes to identifying vulnerable adults?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure most of us remember the case of 26-year-old Annie Ee Yu Lian, who had intellectual disabilities and suffered torture at the hands of a trusted couple.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Eight months of agony and suffering, and yet no one knew – no one even suspected that something was wrong.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How else can we educate Singaporeans to look over one another and be bold enough to report?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is there any other hotline to report suspicion as many may hesitate to report to the Police as it is not yet known to be a fact that such abuse is taking place in the first place?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, some may want to report but do not want their identity to be known for fear of souring their relationship with neighbours, relatives or friends.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can MSF do more to create awareness amongst the public, riding on SG Cares, which is a national movement to support the efforts in building a more caring and inclusive society?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Four, even if a deputy or donee has been appointed, their consent is not required for the power to assess, power to remove and for the medical care to take place as stated in sections 6(2), 10(2) and 18(3) of the Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Under the Mental Capacity Act, however, their consent is required for medical care.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On relocating vulnerable adults, I have the following question.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: MSF is given the mandate to arrange for temporary care location.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, I am optimistic that with the support and cooperation of Singaporeans at large, complemented by robust law and SG Cares initiatives, we can minimise or perhaps eliminate such inhumane abuse and exploitation inflicted upon vulnerable individuals who trust the very people that cause them pain.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having encountered vulnerable adults and their families in my Henderson Dawson Division, I feel this Bill is very timely.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are more people who live longer lives but not always able to care for themselves for one reason or another and becomes vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am pleased to note that the Bill aims to provide a safe environment for whistleblowers to report abuse and suspected abuse to the authorities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One common reason the neighbours and even relatives and co-workers do not lodge reports is because they are afraid that they will be identified.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But this will pose a challenge under certain circumstances if the authorities decide to take the abuser to Court where evidence from witnesses are required.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is most crucial is that the evidence deduced from the whistleblower, and evidence thrown up in the Police investigations, such as the injuries sustained by the victim, are the critical factors in the case in convicting the accused person(s).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, abuse and neglect often occur when the caregivers are at wit's end.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We all would know how difficult it is to handle individuals when they suffer from mental distress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The person may refuse to eat, bathe, take medication, may throw tantrums, create a ruckus and disturb his or her neighbours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On some days, as early as 5.00 am, my resident – let us call him Mr S – gets up and yells vulgarities very loudly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr S lives with his spouse, and the family puts in effort to get him treatment and to take his medication.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The spouse does her best to make sure Mr S takes his medicine regularly and the VWOs assist when she cannot.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it is not working out and she has sort of given up.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Meantime, the neighbours suffer along with the family.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Still, there is a need to find a solution.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, a lot would depend on what resources there are available to the family.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hospitals would not keep an individual in the ward unless there is a medical need to do so.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Caregiving homes and hospice care may be out of reach for some and some fall through the cracks as they do not meet the per capita income for Government help but are unable to afford on their income level.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Here is where the family members need help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The family members must work, yet the distressed person needs their care and attention.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would help to lighten their load to know who and where they can get help to meet their needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An intervention by a Government agency can save the distressed individual from being relegated from being a loved one to becoming a burden to the family.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Once they are seen as a burden, then that is where the person becomes vulnerable to abuses of all kinds.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are many cases where because of the pull between filial piety and financial affordability, the relationship between husband and wife becomes strained, or relations between brothers and sisters become strained.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Accusations and finger-pointing create quarrels and you see a family divided.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I know it is heart-wrenching for the family.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: No one wants to "abandon" their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, although this Bill is targeted at vulnerable adults, similar problems can be observed in children with health problems requiring extensive care, as well as their parents, caregivers and neighbours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similar intervention and help should also be extended to such families.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I have always been concerned about the vulnerable adults and have, since 1999, raised the issue on better protection of our vulnerable adults and, especially the abused seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I have spoken about the predicament of vulnerable adults being abused and have beseeched our Government to better assist them at least nine times in this House.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad, indeed, that MSF will soon put into law to better safeguard the vulnerable adults.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, during my speeches on this topic, I have raised the issues of neglect of the vulnerable, physical abuse resulting in injuries, emotional trauma, psychological anguish, deceit of funds and financial abuse.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to address financial abuse in these vulnerable adults.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them would have some savings from their long working years and they may be subjected to financial abuse.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will be an increasing problem with time.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I have heard residents and patients relating to me that they had to give in reluctantly to their difficult children who might be drug abusers, ex-convicts or gamblers when they demanded money from them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The seniors said they were afraid of their children; scared of their tantrums, tempers and abusive words if they did not give in.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There were also stories of unpaid borrowings by children, deceit in transferring of HDB ownership and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, this Bill is not complete with the omission of the financial abuse issue.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: During one of my house visits, I saw one debilitated senior on her bed through her house gate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: She was too weak to even sit up or talk to us.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Her gate was locked by her only son when he left to work early in the morning and would only come back late at night.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I considered it as a case of neglect, either due to circumstances or willfully.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: But the senior would not complain as she was too afraid to lose whatever she had left and had resigned to her fate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thankfully, we managed to find her son and persuaded him to allow us to assist with his mother's daily needs and medical needs henceforth.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope this Bill will enable individuals like this to be identified early and help rendered before it is too late.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The role of the community is important to better protect the vulnerable adults.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Extended families and neighbours are usually the first to know of the vulnerable adults at risk.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This fact must be well publicised to encourage more people in the community to report.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In publicity materials, tips on what to look out for will be useful to further raise the awareness.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Such relevant information includes poor hygiene, malnutrition, dehydration, physical injuries like bruises and fractures, unexpected injuries, mental trauma, depression as well as social isolation.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The people in the community, the family and friends as well as the neighbours, and the frontline personnel, such as medical doctors, nurses and social workers, play an important role to ensure the success of this Bill when it is enacted.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In our society, there is a strong disapproval of abuses, especially so on the vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope MSF will spare no effort in facilitating the community to play their part in our responsible and caring society.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a need for easy one-stop reporting and good follow-up provided by MSF.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The convenience of a designated 24-hour hotline to call for reporting on information will be useful.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that with this Act and the good execution efforts by MSF, we can prevent another case of Ms Annie Ee who died from the injury of frequent abuses over a long period.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Does this Bill send a strong signal to the perpetrators on their wrongdoings?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Now that there is this Act, we need to have a deterrence to ensure that family members do not push their dependants away to MSF by causing neglect.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Otherwise, perpetrators can walk away from their responsibilities, if they know that they can get away easily.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Under Part 3, clause 19(1) and (2) of this Bill, the Minister is empowered, by notification in the Gazette, to designate any premises in Singapore as a place of temporary care and protection for the care of vulnerable adults from abuse, neglect or self-neglect.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In many cases of abuse, the best way to end their plight is to remove the vulnerable from their homes and place them at designated facilities that can provide better support and care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We have to make sure that the vulnerable are not worse off with our intervention.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I also hope that MSF will ensure that the vulnerable adults at risk receive as much information on their alternate care and assistance available to them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The fear of the unknown, away from their familiar environment and the fear of losing whatever little care and support they are getting may prevent the vulnerable adults at risk from giving their consent for interventions involving removal and out-of-home placements.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially so for the seniors at risk.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that MSF will implement this Act thoroughly to ensure its success.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The success of all these will save our vulnerable adults from unnecessary pain and suffering and this is only rightly so in our inclusive caring society.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the course of our daily interactions with others in our community, we would have come across adults who are deemed vulnerable, either because they have some form of special need, or because of age, they suffer from illnesses or conditions that diminish their ability to remember or communicate effectively, such as dementia, aphasia – which is an impairment of the ability to speak because of stroke –or multiple sclerosis, among others.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A few months back, a female resident, Ms N, came to see me at my Meet-the-People session, panicky and in tears.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ms N shared that her elderly father, whom she said had dementia, was missing and that she received a call from a Home for destitute persons informing her that her father was there.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Apparently, he was found begging on the streets and could not recall where he lived.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When Ms N went down to the Home to try and bring her elderly father home, she was told that she could not do so as the Home would need to get the go-ahead from MSF before they could release her father.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She managed to talk to her father whom she said appeared scared and had suicidal thoughts.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I managed to get in touch with MSF through Minister Desmond Lee and, with the Minister's kind help, managed to get Ms N's father released from the Home within the next few days.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I must extend my sincerest gratitude, on behalf of my resident, for the Minister's timely intervention and assistance in this case.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While that incident turned out well for Ms N and her father, the reality remains that there will be adults among us who may not recall who they are or where they live, or who may do things that can compromise their safety or the safety or others.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, for clause 3(2), it is mentioned that the Director may appoint any public officer with suitable qualifications and experience as protector under the proposed Bill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What qualities are needed before a public officer can be appointed as a protector?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the functions and powers of the protector?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is the protector different from the Director?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is the protector a deputy to the Director?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or is the protector supposed to play the role of a counter-check to the Director or enforcement officers to ensure, for example, that the safety of the vulnerable adult is ensured, or that excessive force is not meted on any vulnerable adult that is being removed from a place that exposes that adult to abuse, neglect or self-neglect?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, for clause 6(1)(d) and clause 10(2), it is stated that the Director or protector may remove a vulnerable adult from the place where that vulnerable adult is residing or staying for the purpose of an assessment, with or without the consent of that vulnerable adult, their donee or deputy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To what extent can the Director or protector ensure this vulnerable adult is to be removed?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What if the vulnerable adult becomes hysterical or has an emotional breakdown or a meltdown and starts to protest?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Ministry manage this delicate balance between state intervention and individual rights and choices?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will physical force or coercion be used against this vulnerable adult?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Who will provide that counter-check against the use of excessive physical force or coercion against a vulnerable adult?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be a standard engagement procedure employed when dealing with such adults, where engagement, communication and cajoling are applied first and foremost?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What if the vulnerable adult in question turns violent?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fourth, for clause 11(1)(a), in having removed a vulnerable adult, the Director or protector must commit the vulnerable adult to a place of temporary care and protection or to the care of a fit person.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, for clause 19(1), the Minister may designate any premises in Singapore as a place of temporary care and protection, or as a place of safety for the care and protection of vulnerable adults.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What would be these places of temporary care and protection?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How long will the vulnerable adults be committed to such places of temporary care and protection?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And in terms of "fit persons", how are the competencies and qualities of these "fit persons" defined?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be considerations of prior interaction or relationship to the vulnerable adult in question, so as to ensure some level of familiarity or comfort?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be considerations of prior relevant experience or similar language ability to the vulnerable adult, so as to ensure minimal miscommunication?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fifth, for clauses 20(1) and 20(2), a "proper care plan" has to be in place for a vulnerable adult.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some criteria of the "proper care plan" for vulnerable adults?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will this "proper care plan" be made in consultation with family members should the vulnerable adult be committed to a place of temporary care and protection?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Review Board or Director or protector be the one to review or audit this "proper care plan" on a regular basis to ensure adherence?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I understand that for far too long, social workers have been left frustrated with the inability to take action in situations where they feel that more could be done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note the great balancing act that needs to be put in place to ensure that while we do what we think is necessary for the group that cannot help themselves, we do not inadvertently trample on individual rights and liberties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, although personally, I share the sentiments of some of my colleagues who feel that the Bill could extend to protect against issues like financial abuse, I appreciate the caution with which we proceed on this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that the Ministry would review the matter further and consider other recourse available to the elderly in this respect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For the purposes of this speech though, I would like to focus on the implementation of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my humble opinion, for this Bill to be effectively administered and for the true spirit of the Bill to be embraced, we need to ensure that there are appropriate support, resources and manpower in place to respond to the circumstances that would arise in the course of enforcement of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, what are the measures or support framework in place to ensure reconciliation with families where appropriate?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I know that the Minister had earlier shared that Court orders could be made to direct family members to attend counselling.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are there other mechanisms to assist with reconciliation and appropriate follow-ups with the family members?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, I believe that the cases that would fall under this category would be complicated and potentially emotionally and logistically challenging.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The social welfare officers need to be trained in various aspects.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They should be equipped with skills in dealing with, for example, violent relatives, they need to understand the Court processes and also have greater depth in dealing with and recognising psychological on top of physical harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister could shed some light on the matters I raised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Notwithstanding my request for clarifications, I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some Members suggested identifying vulnerable adults early, to ensure their well-being, to be as proactive as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Thanaletchimi and Ms Denise Phua asked what the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) can do to educate our stakeholders and Singaporeans generally, to report suspected abuse cases that they come across.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, everyone should actively report suspected cases of abuse, neglect and self-neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF launched a three-year "Break the Silence" campaign in late 2016 to encourage open conversations about family violence, including abuse of vulnerable adults, to urge bystanders to action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We went onto social media, we went onto radio, television (TV), cinema screens, outdoor media and roadshows to campaign for greater public awareness that family abuse is not a private matter and cannot be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And, Sir, this has gone some way to shape public attitudes towards family violence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF has also been training community partners and grassroots volunteers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are on the ground and can help us detect formerly "invisible" cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to step up on our efforts in this area, as the work of public education and capacity building can never end.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The whistleblower clauses in this Bill will support both of these efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we want frontline staff in relevant agencies to be well-trained and equipped to identify cases of abuse, neglect and self-neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include our Family Violence Specialist Centres (FVSCs) and Family Service Centres (FSCs) as well as medical and healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To Mr Louis Ng's question on their training, MSF has established protocols and training platforms that equip them to handle and detect family violence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include training modules at the Social Service Institute on identifying and managing vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF is also building on our existing Integrated Family Violence Manual, which agencies rely on to guide their intervention into family violence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This manual will soon also cover the safety of vulnerable adults – so, work in progress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To more effectively identify and help vulnerable adults, MSF is currently working with our community partners to co-develop relevant Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and assessment guides.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, the Government must provide avenues for easy reporting and react quickly to reports that come in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi, Mr Louis Ng and Ms Joan Pereira asked about a public hotline where people can report abuse and neglect of vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if every case of vulnerable adult abuse will be reported to the Police for action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, who should the public call if they come across suspected cases?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They can alert the nearest FSC, they can call any of the three FVSCs set up by MSF, the numbers for both are available on our website, or they can call MSF's ComCare Hotline at 1800-222-0000.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where there are immediate safety concerns or danger to a vulnerable adult, the public can call the Police.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But not every case of harm to vulnerable adults may necessarily warrant Police involvement, at least from the get go.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where the safety concerns are not so clear or immediate, our FSCs and FVSCs will first look into the matter and alert us at MSF if state intervention is necessary and then we will move in together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, professionals have expressed to us concerns that mandatory reporting laws, such as this, especially in a family violent situation, may prevent abusers from seeking help for themselves or their victims, as they fear being taken to task.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we prefer, for now, to assure people who step forward, through whistleblower protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will also be developing protocols and guidelines, similar to those used in the child protection sector, to educate professionals and the public on when, how and who to report such cases to.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, for those Members who are familiar with the Child Protection Scheme, there is a Child Abuse Reporting Guide which we share with our network, preschools, schools, clinics, the Police, medical professionals, hospitals, and using methodical approach, guide them on what to look out for, what to ask and what information to get and who to report to.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we are looking at the same protocol for adult abuse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Denise Phua recommended forming a National Vulnerable Adults Support Services Association.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It sounds very much like our Community Network for Seniors where we rely on community and partners and people on the ground to form networks to look after seniors and, in this case, to look after vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We thank her for her suggestion and we will certainly explore this in greater detail.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked why the Bill only protects vulnerable adults aged 18 and older.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: How about legal protection for those above 16 but below 18, since the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA) only covers individuals below 16?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, vulnerable individuals, aged 16 to 18, have some protection under existing legislation, such as the Women's Charter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Women's Charter protects individuals, regardless of their gender and age, from family violence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A number of Members, including Dr Lily Neo, asked why the Bill does not cover financial abuse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, many of the Members have come across cases where parents have provided for the children, sold their homes and helped their children buy their new homes only to find themselves ejected out of those homes, or to be financially abused in any other case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Daniel Goh that cases of financial abuse often involve elements of psychological and emotional abuse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, where financial abuse occurs alongside other forms of abuse and neglect that are already covered under the Bill, the state can intervene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are also some other levers in place to deal with financial abuse against vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In cases where vulnerable adults have been exploited by caregivers, we often do see other family members, such as children, stepping forward to put a firm stop to this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If need be, our social work agencies can nudge next-of-kin to act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Criminal charges or criminal investigation are not the only ways by which the Public Guardian can apply to Court to take action, again in cognisance of other facts, such as the donee or deputy not acting in the best interest of the elderly person, including financially abusing the elderly person.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, family members can also make such an application to Court.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the vulnerable adult lacks mental capacity and has no family members, a deputy may be appointed by the Court to manage his property and affairs as well as his personal welfare matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The professional deputy will be subject to the same requirements as any other deputy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the caregiver who financially abuses the vulnerable adult is neither a donee nor deputy, MSF and our partners will carry out social work interventions and assessments to look at what the situation is about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We may ask the Public Guardian to step in to ask for the Court to appoint a deputy to look into the vulnerable adult's financial situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Again, this is also open to next-of-kin to do so, to solve this problem within the family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Let us gain more experience in operationalising this vulnerable adult protection framework, while we continue to study the complex issue of financial exploitation among family members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members have raised ideas to us in the course of this debate and the recent Motion on protecting our seniors and, of course, in many other debates and other platforms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Let us continue to look at them and, at an appropriate time, we will bring it to this House.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why the Bill does not define sexual abuse as an independent head of abuse, and how it considers verbal sexual harassment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sexual offences are covered under the Penal Code, for example.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If there is conduct or behaviour that coerces or attempts to coerce an individual to engage in sexual activity, this is "physical abuse" under the Bill, and action can be taken.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For verbal sexual harassment, this can fall under "emotional or psychological abuse".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong asked why the definitions of "emotional or psychological abuse", "neglect" and "self-neglect" are definitive, as compared to the definition of "physical abuse" which is non-exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Physical abuse already has a limiting factor, in that the abuse must be physical in nature.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is unlikely to be largely differing views on what would constitute physical abuse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is less clear for emotional and psychological abuse, neglect or even self-neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There may be differing opinions among professionals as well as members of the public on what these would constitute.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These definitions are, therefore, crafted definitively, to provide as much clarity and certainty as possible on who the powers in the Bill apply to, and limit our discretion on how these terms are interpreted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong also asked why psychological assessment was not included in the definition of "assessment" under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The current definition of "assessment" allows interviews and examinations to be conducted to determine a person's mental state.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This allows psychologists or psychiatrists to interview and examine a vulnerable adult to ascertain if there are any psychological concerns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, Deputy Speaker, let me take a step back from all the points that have been raised, whether on financial abuse or on the definitions of abuse, neglect or self-neglect, and assure Members that these scope the statutory powers that we can exercise under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The FSC, FVSC and our Adult Protective Service (APS) and our Rehabilitation and Protection Group (RPG) units in MSF are not prevented from social work interventions, reaching to the family, reaching out to the community, reaching out to neighbours, reaching out to the vulnerable adult because of the scope of definitions in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If there is a concern, our community and social work agencies and MSF will respond with social work as our primary tool, but as far as the exercise of these intrusive statutory powers are concerned, then we are limited by the definitions under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I hope Members understand that these definitions and the scope of the Bill do not prevent us from acting as we have always done, both now and in the past.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Denise Phua asked about how the Bill will complement existing services, including that by APS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asked about the qualities required of protectors and their roles under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the similarities and differences between APS and Child Protective Service (CPS).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The principles guiding APS and CPS' work are similar in that the best interest and welfare of the vulnerable adult and child respectively must be paramount.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Beyond the distinct age groups each Service looks after, APS' work requires them to look into the vulnerable adult's mental capacity so that the client's right to self-determination is upheld as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This leads me to Ms Denise Phua and Ms Sylvia Lim's question on how MSF decides when to intervene, and the rigour of our assessment, particularly when we remove a vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I agree with both of them that mental incapacity is a continuum, and that mental capacity is not a black-and-white concept.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, there are good days and there are bad days.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will be confirmed by a qualified assessor who can conduct physical and mental capacity assessments or it might be different assessors would have come in together and do the assessments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assessing the mental capacity of a vulnerable adult is important because, as far as possible, an adult with the capacity to make decisions should do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To ensure that we protect his right to participate in the decision-making process, MSF has been working with our partners to develop a mental capacity assessment form.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This form sets out certain requirements and checklists that will determine if a vulnerable adult lacks mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, if the vulnerable adult is unable to understand information that is relevant to the decision at hand, to retain that information or to communicate his decision to others, then he will be considered as lacking mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On Ms Denise Phua's example, where the vulnerable adult has mental capacity but shows signs of self-neglect, MSF can intervene to protect him from further neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On Ms Sylvia Lim's examples, MSF will not remove a vulnerable adult without assessing the situation holistically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In such cases, we will work with our social service agencies and other agencies to provide assistance to the family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim had given examples of cases where a person fulfills the example in the illustration but in her view and certainly in mine, I should not invoke a removal of the adult, for example, if the vulnerable adult is unclothed after a bath but the caregiver needs to go and prepare some medication, for instance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This would not be the way in which APS and our agencies act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It would involve concerns being raised; it would involve interviews, talking to the caregiver, talking to the family members, talking to the neighbours, speaking to the community, speaking to the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not a case of looking at a snapshot of facts that within these 10 seconds, what you did and, therefore, I come and use these powers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That would not really be within the ambit of how we do social work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And as I mentioned in my opening speech, we will be judicious in how we exercise the powers under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When we identify a vulnerable adult, the default, where possible, should be to rely on social suasion with the support of his family and the community, because that approach is often more effective and sustainable, internalised by the vulnerable adult and the family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Only when this is ineffective, will we rely on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the state's power to remove, Ms Chia Yong Yong said that MSF should be able to remove a vulnerable adult for assessment of placement if there are reasonable grounds to believe that an adult is withholding consent due to some form of coercion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Other Members felt that we should be more judicious in the exercise of powers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Again, as Ms Chia Yong Yong has rightly pointed out, it is a matter of perspective, whether you are focusing on the needs of the vulnerable adult or whether you are concerned about whether there is statutory overreach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I agree that a vulnerable adult’s right to self-determination should be respected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is why we hardwired this as one of the key principles in the Bill, and also why there are safeguards in the Bill against unnecessary intervention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But there may be exceptional situations where intervention may be necessary even when the vulnerable adult has mental capacity and refuses assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Ms Chia Yong Yong highlighted, there may be instances where the adult is under duress or pressured by their loved ones to refuse external assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I also mentioned the case of Mr Wong earlier, the elderly man who refused admission to a hospital or nursing home to treat his diabetes and wounds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is a real risk that Mr Wong's life will be in danger in the future, if the state cannot intervene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where there are reasonable grounds to believe that a suspected vulnerable adult is withholding consent because of coercion or undue influence, for example, we will bring this to the Court's attention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Court can then make an order for MSF to intervene to protect the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If there are concerns whether it is expeditiously enough, especially where the case is particularly urgent, then there are provisions in the Bill that allow ex-parte application.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asked if engagement and communication should be applied first before we invoke the law to remove a vulnerable adult, while Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked if MSF can exercise some of its powers under the Bill while family and community interventions are ongoing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Allow me to reiterate that family engagement and social work intervention by community partners, supported by MSF, will be the principal response to cases involving vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But statutory intervention and family or community interventions are not mutually exclusive and there may be times when a combination is necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To Dr Intan Mokhtar's questions on how a vulnerable adult will be removed from his place of residence, if this is necessary, MSF is currently developing its SOPs to guide the actions of officers when dealing with vulnerable adults, including removal from their homes, where understanding and training are absolutely key.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To ensure that the experience does not traumatise the vulnerable adult, MSF will engage the help of support persons, which may include social workers, psychologists and community partners who have interacted with the adult, to assist with this removal.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Friends and close family members may also be present as a form of assurance and support for him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some Members raised questions about care facilities and arrangements for vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, Dr Intan Mokhtar and Dr Lily Neo asked which premises will be gazetted as places of temporary care and protection and how long a vulnerable adult would reside in these premises.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A few medical facilities may also be gazetted to cater to situations where the vulnerable adults have clear medical needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These facilities are intended to protect vulnerable adults who cannot remain safely in their place of residence, while allowing them to receive appropriate care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The choice of gazetted care facilities and period of committal will depend on a vulnerable adult's care needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Again, this depends on specific circumstances of the vulnerable adult and the family or lack thereof.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, Ms Denise Phua asked whether these facilities and staff are equipped to care for vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These facilities have experience providing for residents who are vulnerable and have in place suitable standards of care to provide for their care and protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said earlier, MSF is also working with frontline officers of relevant agencies to ensure that they have the capabilities to provide support to vulnerable adults under their care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, Dr Intan Mokhtar also asked how the competencies and qualities of a "fit person" are defined, and about the care plan that will be put in place if a vulnerable adult is committed to a facility. "Fit persons" are individuals or organisations whom the Director of Social Welfare thinks are competent to provide care and protection to the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The main consideration as to whether one qualifies to be a fit person is whether he has the ability to provide the necessary care and protection to ensure the vulnerable adult’s safety and allow him to recuperate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, a fit person could actually be a family member or a friend who is willing and able to care for the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for care plans, MSF will put them in place to ensure that the vulnerable adult receives the care and protection he requires while in the facility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The care plan sets out a care and recovery framework based on a comprehensive assessment of the vulnerable adult’s social, mental and physical state.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF, together with a Review Board comprising professionals, will review these plans regularly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fourth, Dr Intan Mokhtar asked whether family members are allowed to visit vulnerable adults in gazetted facilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, they are allowed and encouraged to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF may also limit the contact between the vulnerable adult residing in gazetted facilities and individuals if such contact does not serve the best interest of the adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also provided several suggestions to help vulnerable adults adjust to their new environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I note her suggestions and we will explore these ideas with the management of the facilities to ensure that these vulnerable adults feel safe and comfortable even while they are there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fifth, Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Seah Kian Peng asked who will bear the costs of the care of a vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, if families have the means, the costs of placement and any other services or treatment of the vulnerable adult requires should be borne by them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we recognise that not all families can provide for their vulnerable family members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sixth, Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about reintegration of vulnerable adults with their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The vulnerable adult will only return home after we deem it is safe for him to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will then work with a community agency to monitor the case and provide necessary support, until it is assessed that no further risks exist.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Daniel Goh that the Government must exercise restraint before interfering with family prerogatives with regard to a vulnerable adult’s personal care arrangements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where possible, MSF will help facilitate the family in caring for their vulnerable members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This may include the provision of social support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Several Members, including Ms Denise Phua, asked about the Bill’s interface with other legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill complements the existing legal framework that protects vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As the Bill covers a wider scope of vulnerable individuals, there will inevitably be some overlap.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But the Bill will, ultimately, strengthen the current framework by allowing MSF to take a more proactive approach to protecting vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF can only do our work when we have the support of the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will work with community partners to put in place robust protocols.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If practitioners based in the community are unsure, they can approach MSF and we will advise them on the best approach to take in relation to that particular case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This already happens on the ground and will remain so, going forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I now move to Ms Sylvia Lim’s question on whether a complaint against a donee or deputy should be made to the Director of Social Welfare under the Bill, or to the Public Guardian under the Mental Capacity Act (MCA).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill overlaps with the MCA in that both protect vulnerable adults who lack mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But both Bill and the Act complement each other and strengthen the protection afforded to these vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Vulnerable Adults Bill allows the state to intervene swiftly to assess and remove a vulnerable adult to safety and apply for the necessary Court orders to ensure his protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The MCA then allows the Office of the Public Guardian to intervene, by applying to Court if the powers of the vulnerable adult’s donee or deputy need to be suspended or revoked to prevent further abuse of the adult and, if necessary, another deputy brought in, or a professional deputy, as the case may be.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where such incidents occur, it actually does not really quite matter to whom the complaint about the donee or deputy was made.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF, including our APS and the Office of the Public Guardian, will have to assess each complaint holistically before determining the next steps.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked if there is any conflict between the MCA and the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While a donee or deputy appointed under the MCA can give or withhold consent to treat a vulnerable adult, the MCA actually already allows for doctors or dentists to override the donee’s or deputy’s decision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This occurs when the person providing healthcare reasonably believes that treatment is necessary to prevent serious deterioration of the adult's condition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A similar principle now applies in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In such situations, we have allowed for treatment to be administered, as withholding treatment would, in such circumstances, go against the best interests of the vulnerable adult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act (MHCTA) will operate in relation to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Not all vulnerable adults will fall under MHCTA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, not all vulnerable adults suffer from mental disorders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of the vulnerable adults that APS sees today may only suffer from physical disability or infirmity but not mental disorder.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, not all vulnerable adults should be admitted to a psychiatric institution when found to be suffering from ill-treatment or neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some, with mental disorders, may benefit more from living in a gazetted care facility or with a fit person, and may even be able to live alone, as these arrangements may better meet their care needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Again, it is very specific to the individual's case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Others may actually be able to live alone and just require protection from the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In such cases, a protection order may be applied for to ensure the vulnerable adult’s safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Women’s Charter protects individuals of all ages from violence committed by family members.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In cases of family violence, individuals can apply for a protection order against the perpetrator under the Women’s Charter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we recognise that there may be situations where victims of family violence, after prolonged or intense abuse, may become physically or mentally incapacitated, or both.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have mentioned earlier, the public as well as community agencies can approach MSF and we will review all reports holistically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Joan Pereira raised the issue of caregiver support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I agree with her that caregiver support is important.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Caregivers can face tremendous stress caring for vulnerable family members and, indeed, family matters which involve family violence and abuse are not always black-and-white.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
