text: In the case of Sam, which I described earlier, the vulnerable adult is a 29-year-old man who is both a victim but, in a way, also the cause of the tremendous stress on the part of his father.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For caregivers of vulnerable seniors, they can reach out to the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) as they provide coordinated support to families with vulnerable adults and help them to access care services and schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is the AIC's Silver Line for information on referrals to services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Caregivers can also approach the AICareLinks at hospitals and their office at Maxwell Road.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are one-stop resource centres for caregivers to get information and advice on the appropriate services for their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are several support services that the Government has put in place for vulnerable adults and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we have centre-based care services where seniors can receive care during the day.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes day care, dementia day care and day rehabilitation services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, respite care options are also available so that caregivers can take a break.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They can opt to send their family members to eldercare centres for a few hours on weekends so that caregivers can recharge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For caregivers who need a slightly longer break of several days to a few weeks, they can tap on nursing home respite care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fourth, Foreign Domestic Worker Levy Concessions are also available for those who need to hire a domestic helper at home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For caregivers of persons with disabilities, they can also reach out to SG Enable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Support for caregivers range from day care to long-term residential care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They include the Drop-in Disability Programme – these are centres located within the community that provide social activities to higher functioning persons with disabilities who are able to travel to the centre independently for a few half-day sessions per week.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Day Activity Centres (DACs), which are day programmes to equip persons with disabilities with daily and community living skills and provide care relief for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Adult Disability Hostels (ADHs) are available as alternative housing arrangements for adults with disabilities who do not require institutional care but are unable to live with their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And VWO Transport Subsidies are also available for persons with disabilities who need to take dedicated transport provided by VWOs to access care services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked how we can better stay in touch with vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF remains committed to working with families and community partners to build capabilities and competencies to support vulnerable adults and to detect abuse or neglect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Therefore, while we seek to operationalise the Bill, the Government has already been working on strengthening the social-health integration framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will build even tighter networks with Government agencies, FSCs, SSOs, VWOs and other community partners to improve work processes and share information relating to the needs of our seniors and persons with disability that will help close the gaps in the adult protection landscape.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, MSF has transferred our functions under the Senior Cluster Networks, such as the Senior Activity Centres (SACs), Cluster Support, Caring Assistance from Neighbours (CANs) and other programmes, such as befriending services, over to MOH.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will allow MOH to bring a host of preventive health and healthcare services that will twin the social support provided by the SACs to seniors in rental precincts and studio apartments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include exercises and nutritional programmes, chronic and functional screening, as well as nursing posts set up at the SACs to help seniors better manage their health conditions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, with the merger of the Silver Generation Office (SGO) with AIC, SGO has trained our Silver Generation Ambassadors (SGAs) to proactively reach out to, and identify both social as well as health risks and needs among our elderly, and encourage seniors to step out of their homes to participate in preventive health screening and active ageing programmes to draw them away from social isolation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through this effort, AIC links up different Government agencies and community partners to sew up care across both the health and social domains for seniors, especially those living alone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In particular, AIC works with various community-based organisations and grassroots organisations to recruit and train befrienders to look out for seniors living alone in the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where SGAs or grassroots leaders identify vulnerable seniors, AIC will coordinate both social and health support from various Government agencies and community partners to help them and, there, the SSOs and the Silver Generation officers will work very closely on the ground in the local communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes financial assistance, aged care services and health services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Similarly, if persons with disabilities are identified to have unmet needs, they will be linked up to the relevant agencies, such as SG Enable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, MOH has integrated home and day care packages, as well as home medical, home nursing, home therapy and home personal care services, to support seniors more holistically so that they can age in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With this framework in place, the Government will be able to tap on the skills and the networks in different sectors to ensure a more robust support system is in place for vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Henry Kwek called for a stronger push for LPA adoption to prepare our society for potential loss of mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Office of the Public Guardian has embarked on a Business Process Re-engineering (BPR) exercise precisely to enable us to be future-ready in protecting our seniors who may lose mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An interagency workgroup has been formed to do this, and will consult the public and stakeholders, and I will ask the workgroup to work and study Mr Kwek's ideas further.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Family Justice Courts, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) and MSF had convened the Committee to Review and Enhance Reforms in the Family Justice System (RERF) in January this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: More details will be provided when the Committee finalises its recommendations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will also continue exploring ways to ensure that the vulnerable among us are supported.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where eligible, a vulnerable adult could be supported under the Community Kin pilot, where VWOs can apply for a Court order to manage small and specific sums of an adult’s money for his day-to-day needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will enable the vulnerable adult to remain in the community with assistance from existing care networks, rather than have to be prematurely institutionalised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Louis Ng have asked why it took three years for the Bill to be introduced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This Bill involves intrusive statutory intervention in the realm of family and personal matters, so we did not want to rush this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, as a Member has pointed out – was it Assoc Prof Daniel Goh – this Bill heralds more conversations in the future about the extent to which external state power should be brought into the realm of the family to enable, intervene and support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, this is not just a Bill that involves operational details.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It does involve quite a lot of that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But also very fundamental questions that we have to debate both internally and with our stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We had to consult our stakeholders extensively and review how past cases were handled to see where the law needed to come in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In drawing up the Bill, we had detailed discussions with public agencies and community partners, such as our FVSCs, FSCs, SSOs, hospitals, the Police, the Courts and so on, on implementation, on SOPs – and work is still in progress on that front – capabilities, resourcing and training, not to mention the philosophical discussions that we have to have with various partners who are concerned about whether the Bill was sufficiently interventionist or whether it is overly intrusive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And, of course, during all this time, it was not the case that vulnerable adults were not supported and abuse left unattended.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Social work intervention by our FSCs, FVSCs, SSC Cluster support, our APS, RPG, Office of the Public Guardian, AIC and the Police continues, as they have always been doing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With this Bill, we hope to be able to add on to that framework with the suite of powers that we are seeking your support on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I think he mentioned that the Government is reviewing raising the age in the Children and Young Persons' Act from 16 to 18.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to ensure that there is seamless protection for both children and vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And this is something that we will do.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The Minister mentioned in response to my suggestion for mandatory reporting that overseas jurisdictions showed that there was a case that when you have that, it leads to over-reporting.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: But why I proposed that was because I felt it is better to err on the side of caution.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: If there is no mandatory reporting, we will suffer the other consequence that there will be under-reporting.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I also note that the Minister said, therefore, he is relying more on whistleblowing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: That being the case, I would urge the Minister and the Ministry to really step up so that this whistleblowing awareness is a lot heightened because I am worried that under-reporting will lead to real consequences for the vulnerable adults.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, as I have said earlier, a mandatory scheme was, indeed, considered by MSF.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There was considerable concern by professionals as to the efficacy and necessity of a mandatory reporting scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we adopted this where we strengthen and expand our network of care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Just like in child protection and adult protection, you also have to rely on a wide range of partners, both the community services, as well as professionals in healthcare and elsewhere that we share with them the importance of reporting suspected cases of abuse, that we guide them on what to look out for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let us put this whistleblower framework in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But let us look at it in the future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: So, I would like to understand a little more about what steps will be taken.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Will the Government also be prepared to look into amendments and steps to overturn even established principles of law, such as presumption of advancement and so on, for the protection of vulnerable elderly persons?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: My second clarification relates again to the definitions which I had earlier submitted were far too narrow.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The Minister clarified that by scoping the definitions, there is greater clarity for the exercise of the powers by the Director.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: On the other hand, the scoping of the definitions also means that the Director may be less able to exercise discretion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: So, I would like to know how the Director would be able to balance considerations of protection and also in relation to applications for expedited orders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member had given some very useful ideas at the last Motion debate on seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If I recall, there were five ideas that the Member had raised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are studying each and every one of them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members, over the course of debates in the last few years, have also raised concerns about financial abuse of the elderly and abuse of parents financially.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is something that we continue to look at.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are existing frameworks, such as the Commissioner of Maintenance of Parents and the Tribunal for the Maintenance of Parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members who come across cases where even though an elderly constituent comes to tell you that he has been financially abused, when you offer some suggestions, they would not want to act on them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They do not want services to come in, they do not want you to report to the Tribunal for the Maintenance of Parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They do not want the FSCs to get involved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a complex family and personal matter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it is not a trivial matter, and I am sure Members will continue to look at possible solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As to the point about whether long-established principles we are prepared to overturn, we will look at what can work and what will be acceptable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The other question is about the scoping of definitions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, the Member has articulated that kind of balance we have had to strike between on the one hand having clarity and giving assurance that these interventionist powers will be limited to a very clearly defined scope and, on the other hand, always fearing that if you scope things too definitively and do not have discretion, for example, if the definition does not say "it includes" but it is not definitive, it includes other things as well, that you might just miss that opportunity to act in that one right case as it is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let us develop experience operationalising these powers and then we can continue to review whether there are gaps that need to be plugged in the future.
